title: The car-ride counting game: numbers one to ten in two languages, no screen
description: Turn the school run into number practice: pick one thing to count out of the window, count it to ten in the language you are building, then let your child choose the next thing.
book_line: Bilingual English-Spanish vocabulary book for kids: themed word lists and simple activities, read on a Kindle, copied into a notebook when you want them on paper.
pin_title: The car-ride counting game: numbers one to ten in two languages, no screen
body:
Car and bus rides are dead time for a child in a seat: they cannot move, and they are looking out of the window anyway. A counting game uses exactly that.

Pick one thing to count. It should be common on your route but not constant: dogs, bicycles, trees with no leaves, red doors. One thing per trip keeps it simple.

Count out loud in the language you are building, up to ten. If Spanish is the one you are building: "¡un perro!… dos perros… tres perros". If it is English: "one dog… two dogs… three dogs". Your child spots, and you count together. One small Spanish detail you can just model: "uno" becomes "un" before a masculine word (un perro) and "una" before a feminine one (una bicicleta). When you reach ten, the round is over and the spotter chooses the next thing to count.

A safety note that matters more than the game: if you are driving, you only talk. Your child does the spotting and the pointing; your eyes stay on the road. Pause the game at any tricky junction — it will still be there afterwards.

Three variations once the basic game works.

Count down instead of up. Start at ten and count down each time you spot one — "diez, nueve, ocho" or "ten, nine, eight". The last number can be timed for the moment you arrive.

Split the languages between people. One of you counts in one language, the other answers in the other, taking turns: "uno" — "two" — "tres" — "four". It sounds chaotic, children find it very funny, and every number gets said in both languages.

Guess first. Before leaving, everyone guesses how many dogs you will see on the way. Guessing a number is saying a number.

Leave the numbers above ten for later. Once one to ten is easy in both directions, eleven to twenty is the next step, but there is no rush: a game that stays easy is a game children ask for.

What to avoid: quizzing, as in "what's seven in Spanish?" or "how do you say siete?". A question with one right answer turns the back seat into a classroom. Counting together gets the same numbers said without the test.

No claims about fluency, test scores or developmental outcomes

semantic_review: English body; numbers and short noun phrases in Spanish with correct agreement (un perro, una bicicleta, dos perros). Driver-safety line included. Regional words for car and bus avoided in Spanish.
claims_check: No outcome promises. The text says what to do and how long it takes; it does not claim fluency, school results or cognitive benefits.
